name: Deslorelin
lead: Deslorelin is a synthetic gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) superagonist used mainly in veterinary medicine, sold under names such as Suprelorin, Ovuplant and Sucromate Equine.[1] It is used to control reproduction in animals, for example to promote ovulation in mares and, as a slow-release implant, for reversible contraception in dogs and ferrets.[1][5][6]

Its appearance relevance runs through hormones: GnRH agonists suppress the reproductive axis and thereby sex-steroid levels, which is why this drug class is used in children with precocious puberty to slow bone maturation and preserve adult height. In the National Institutes of Health programme, children treated with deslorelin or histrelin reached a final height above their pre-treatment prediction.[2]
In humans deslorelin has been studied in research settings only, and it is not approved for general human use.[1] No studies have examined it for cosmetic or muscle outcomes.
infobox: Rx-only in the EU; not approved for general human use [1]

paras: Reviews describe deslorelin as widely used for managing reproduction in animals, chiefly to trigger ovulation in mares and to suppress the reproductive axis with implants.[3][5] Studies report reversible long-term suppression of reproductive function in male and female dogs and reversible contraception in male dogs using an implant formulation.[6][8] In horses, Ovuplant was an early deslorelin acetate product; Sucromate Equine was approved by the FDA for horses in November 2010.[1]

A 2018 review of GnRH-agonist slow-release implants in exotic companion animals reports them as an increasingly popular alternative to surgical contraception, effective in ferrets, rats, chickens, psittacines and iguanas and less effective in male guinea pigs, rabbits, veiled chameleons, slider turtles and leopard geckos.[14] A randomized trial examined a GnRH agonist implant as an alternative to surgical neutering in pet ferrets, and reviews cover its use in birds and rodents.[15][16][17] Cat studies used deslorelin implants to postpone puberty and compared GnRH agonist with antagonist in kittens.[18][19]

Wikipedia also lists use in pet parrots with chronic egg laying and for benign prostate hyperplasia in dogs.[1] A clinical trial titled for hair cycle arrest in intact male dogs examined deslorelin for a coat-related condition.[20]

Deslorelin was among the GnRH agonists used in long-term National Institutes of Health work on precocious puberty. The report covered 98 children who reached final adult height after about six years of deslorelin or histrelin treatment starting around age five; in the 80 girls, final height averaged 159.8 cm, above the pretreatment predicted 149.3 cm but below mid-parental height.[2] Registered trials have also looked at it in boys with precocious puberty, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, short stature and BRCA mutation carriers at high breast cancer risk.[10][11][12][13]

Wikipedia's general article on precocious puberty reports that GnRH agonists slow growth velocity and skeletal maturation, that a 2009 consensus found a positive effect on adult height with the greatest benefit when puberty starts before age 6, and that bone mineral density falls during treatment and recovers afterward.[21]

As a GnRH agonist, continuous delivery paradoxically suppresses fertility, while its initial effect is a stimulating flare of the pituitary [3]. Like other peptide drugs it is unstable in gastrointestinal fluids, which is why implants or injections are used [4]. Slow-release gel and implant formulations have been tested in cattle and dogs [8][9].

Wikipedia notes that deslorelin, unlike other GnRH agonists used mainly for downregulation, is used in horses chiefly for its initial flare and resulting LH surge, and lists a molar mass of about 1,282 g/mol.[1] Primate and lemur studies have examined its effect on testosterone, testicular volume and reproductive activity.[22][23]

Ovuplant was withdrawn from the US market after mares that did not conceive failed to return to estrus on time; Sucromate Equine was FDA-approved for horses in November 2010.[1] Development for several human indications, including endometriosis, polycystic ovary syndrome, precocious puberty, prostate cancer and uterine fibroids, was reported discontinued by 2001, with phase III work in prostate cancer.[1]
Approved versions remain marketed in Australia and New Zealand, and the drug is prescription-only in the EU.[1]

Human studies are limited to GnRH-agonist trials in children with precocious puberty and other endocrine conditions, in which deslorelin was one of the agents used.[2][7][10][11][12][13] A long-term follow-up compared reproductive axis recovery in girls with hypothalamic hamartoma and idiopathic precocious puberty after discontinuing GnRH analog treatment.[7] A phase 2 trial combined deslorelin with low-dose add-back estradiol and testosterone in high-risk premenopausal women, and a phase 3 trial examined a three-drug regimen in congenital adrenal hyperplasia.[12][13] No studies found on cosmetic or muscle outcomes.

card.summary: A veterinary GnRH-agonist implant with some pediatric endocrine research; nothing tests it for looks.
card.note: Veterinary drug; not approved for general human use.

quick.overview:
Deslorelin is a lab-made GnRH agonist mostly sold for animals, such as implants that suppress fertility in dogs and ferrets or trigger ovulation in horses.

In humans it appears in older research on precocious puberty and other endocrine conditions. No studies address appearance or muscle use.
quick.mechanism: It acts on the pituitary GnRH receptor; continuous exposure suppresses reproductive hormones after an initial surge [3].
quick.risks: Human safety data come from specialist trials in children and patients. It is not approved for general human use, and the veterinary product Ovuplant was withdrawn in the US after fertility-timing problems in mares [1].

chain: Slows sex-steroid-driven bone maturation in children with precocious puberty
More time to grow, with higher final height than predicted
angle.text: In paediatric endocrinology, GnRH agonists including deslorelin were used to delay puberty in children who started it early, and the long-term NIH trial found final heights above the predicted values. This is a medical use in specific diagnoses; it is not a height treatment for people with normal puberty timing.
